A 36-year-old female migrant worker originating from Shanxi Province and living in Guangdong Province presented for tertiary medical evaluation due to a 9-month history of recurrent high fevers, joint swelling, profound fatigue, and progressive unintentional weight loss. Her past medical history was notable only for untreated asthma of 4 years' duration. She reported no domestic animal contacts or sick contacts, and her family history was negative for autoimmune or immunodeficiency disorders.

Over the preceding months, she was evaluated at two different medical centers where laboratory investigations revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 91 g/L, white blood cell count 2.0 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 73 × 10⁹/L), elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein 35 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 59 mm/h, serum ferritin 256 ng/mL), marked hypergammaglobulinemia (serum IgG 53 g/L), and multiple positive autoantibodies including antinuclear antibodies (ANA, titer 1:320), anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA-M2), anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA), and anti-PM-Scl antibodies. Direct Coombs test was positive, and serum complement levels (C3 and C4) were reduced. Hepatic and renal function panels and serum and urine immunofixation electrophoreses (IFE) were normal. Abdominal imaging revealed massive hepatosplenomegaly with a spleen measuring 25 cm in its longitudinal dimension. Two separate bone marrow examinations at outside facilities revealed hypercellular marrow with erythroid hyperplasia and reported no diagnostic clues or malignant infiltration.

Presumed to have systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), she was treated sequentially with high-dose systemic glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, hydroxychloroquine, tofacitinib, and telitacicept (a BLyS/APRIL inhibitor). Despite intensive immunosuppression, low-grade fevers and pancytopenia persisted. Ten days following self-discontinuation of tapered prednisone and cyclosporine, she suffered a relapse of high spiking fevers up to 40.0°C and was admitted for comprehensive evaluation.

On physical examination, the patient appeared chronical ill and emaciated. Temperature was 39.8°C. Abdominal examination revealed massive splenomegaly extending past the umbilicus along with hepatomegaly, without peritoneal signs. Repeat laboratory testing confirmed persistent pancytopenia, elevated ESR, CRP, serum ferritin, and markedly elevated polyclonal IgG. Non-contrast abdominal CT redemonstrated massive hepatosplenomegaly without discrete focal visceral masses.

A 28-year-old male healthcare worker who emigrated from Vietnam 11 years ago presents with a two-month history of fevers, generalized myalgias, and a severe nonproductive cough. He has a history of extensive plaque psoriasis for which he has been treated with subcutaneous adalimumab for over two years. Approximately one month prior to evaluation, he received courses of doxycycline and azithromycin, which resulted in only temporary symptomatic improvement. He is a nonsmoker, has no pets, and has never received the pneumococcal vaccine.

An outpatient evaluation by a pulmonologist three weeks prior included unremarkable blood tests and a normal plain chest radiograph. On evaluation in the clinic, he is non-toxic with a temperature of 37.2°C, blood pressure of 109/73 mmHg, heart rate of 85 beats per minute, and respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute, with clear breath sounds bilaterally. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest performed that day demonstrates a 1.1 cm lobular opacity in the right lower lobe, a moderate right pleural effusion, hilar lymphadenopathy, and a small volume of perihepatic and perisplenic ascites.

He is promptly admitted to the hospital. On admission, his temperature is 39.0°C, blood pressure is 121/87 mmHg, heart rate is 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 97% on ambient air. Physical examination reveals bilateral pulmonary crackles and extensive active psoriatic plaques. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis reveals diffuse nodularity and thickening of the omentum and peritoneal lining associated with ascites.

A 36-year-old previously healthy man residing in Porto Alegre, Brazil, presents with a progressive, intensely pruritic cutaneous eruption. Four days prior to presentation, he had been fishing barefoot in muddy ground adjacent to a freshwater pond. Within 24 hours following this exposure, he developed cutaneous hemorrhagic blisters on his left foot. Over the subsequent 3 days, the eruption evolved into pruritic, linear to serpiginous, erythematous urticarial lesions ascending along the left lower extremity and reaching his left thigh. In addition, new linear urticarial lesions have progressively appeared across his trunk. He denies any systemic symptoms and reports no medication use.

On physical examination, he appears comfortable and vital signs are normal. Dermatologic inspection reveals hemorrhagic blisters on the left foot, accompanied by prominent erythematous, linear-to-serpiginous urticarial plaques extending along the left lower extremity to the left thigh, as well as multiple linear urticarial tracks over the trunk. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Initial baseline laboratory testing demonstrates peripheral blood eosinophilia; complete blood count, routine stool analysis, and partial urine testing show no other abnormalities.

diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In 3 days, such condition evolved into pruritic, linear to serpiginous, erythematous urticarial lesions in the left lower limb and reached his left thigh (Figures 2 and 3). Progressively, some new urticarial, linear lesions appeared in his trunk.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot occurred when the rapid advancement of serpiginous urticarial lesions from the foot to the trunk (larva currens) following freshwater mud exposure, combined with peripheral eosinophilia, prompted empirical ivermectin administration with rapid clinical regression, followed by definitive histopathologic confirmation of nematode larvae within the epidermis.

He had no history of recreational drug use, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, pre-existing renal disease, or systemic vasculitis.

On physical examination, the patient was comatose and febrile with a temperature of 102°F, tachycardic with a pulse rate of 130 beats per minute, and a blood pressure of 140/70 mmHg. Neurological examination revealed bilateral constricted, sluggishly reactive pupils, decerebrate posturing, mild neck rigidity, and bilaterally extensor plantar reflexes without other focal cranial nerve deficits. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal peripheral pulses without bruits or cardiomegaly; respiratory and abdominal examinations were normal.

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a normocytic, normochromic anemia with a hemoglobin of 9.7 g/dL and an MCV of 90 fL, an ESR of 28 mm/hr, and significant thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 75,000/mm³. Serum biochemical testing—including liver function tests, renal function panels, and serum electrolytes—was within normal limits. Urinalysis showed no proteinuria, hematuria, pyuria, or casts. An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for HIV was negative.

An initial two-week trial of inhaled fluticasone dry powder and oral montelukast for suspected allergic asthma yielded no symptomatic improvement.

On physical examination, vital signs and systemic examinations were entirely normal. A plain chest radiograph and pulmonary function tests showed no abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits except for peripheral eosinophilia and a minimally elevated D-dimer level of 600 ng/mL (reference range: 0–500 ng/mL).

A thoracic computed tomography (CT) angiogram was performed to evaluate the cough and elevated D-dimer, demonstrating well-circumscribed, smooth intraluminal filling defects within the left main pulmonary artery, the upper segmental branch of the lingular artery, and the segmental and subsegmental branches of the left lower lobe artery. These filling defects exhibited direct continuity with an 18 × 16 mm nodular opacity. The right pulmonary arterial tree was entirely clear. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left and right ventricular parameters with a systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 25 mmHg and no intracardiac thrombi. Compression ultrasonography of the lower extremities showed no deep venous thrombosis.

case_prompt:
A 69-year-old Japanese woman with a past medical history of subarachnoid hemorrhage was referred to the dermatology department for evaluation of skin eruptions that had been present for 7 months. She had previously undergone a skin histological sampling of her left upper arm at another medical center, where cutaneous T-cell lymphoma had been suspected based on histopathologic findings.

On physical examination at presentation, erythematous papules and small brown nodules were localized to the left side of her chest, left axilla, and left upper arm. The patient reported no subjective symptoms of itching. Thorough examination of her hands, web spaces, and fingers revealed no burrows or tunnels.

Baseline laboratory investigations revealed a white blood cell count of 9,500/μL (reference range, 3,400–7,300/μL) and a serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R) level of 535 U/mL (reference range, 145–519 U/mL). Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Blood eosinophil percentage was normal, and no abnormal circulating peripheral blood lymphocytes were detected. Whole-body 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography and computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) demonstrated no abnormal tracer uptake.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Suspected due to a 7-month duration of non-pruritic nodules, elevated serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor, and dense CD3+/CD4+ dermal lymphoid infiltration on initial biopsy, but ruled out by lack of Pautrier microabscesses, absence of systemic FDG avidity on PET/CT, and discovery of an epidermal mite.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Incidental detection of an epidermal mite within the stratum corneum on immunohistochemical thin sections followed by microscopic confirmation via potassium hydroxide (KOH) examination established the diagnosis of nodular scabies.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In a specimen stained with CD4, a mite was detected within the stratum corneum of the epidermis [Figure 1e]. At her second visit to our department, scabies was diagnosed based on analysis of the nodules in a potassium hydroxide (KOH) test.

case_prompt:
A 30-year-old female laboratory researcher presented to a community hospital with a 4-day history of systemic illness. Her symptoms began with generalized muscle pain, followed by vomiting, chills, and a febrile sensation. Two days after symptom onset, an erythematous rash developed around both knees. She had no significant past medical history, and no family members or coworkers had experienced similar illnesses. She resided in a non-tropical temperate region during the winter season and reported no recent mosquito bites. Her only travel history was a brief trip to Hong Kong one year earlier. Ten days prior to symptom onset, while working in a biosafety level 2 research facility transferring cultured fluid with a syringe and needle, she sustained an accidental needlestick injury to her hand; she immediately washed the wound under running water for 10 minutes and had it disinfected at a local clinic.

On admission examination, her blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate were within normal limits. Her axillary temperature was 37.3°C, indicating a low-grade fever. Physical examination showed a macular rash distributed around both knees; there was no peripheral edema or abdominal ascites.

Initial laboratory evaluation demonstrated a white blood cell count of 3,390/mm³ with mild leukopenia, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, hematocrit 41.0%, and a platelet count of 300,000/mm³. Serum chemistry showed aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 33 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 26 IU/L, total protein 7.7 g/dL, and albumin 4.3 g/dL, all within reference ranges. Urinalysis was normal.

A 32-year-old male with a history of childhood poliomyelitis presents to a tertiary care medical center with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging, painless deep perianal mass accompanied by intermittent chronic constipation. He was referred for evaluation of a suspected retroperitoneal sarcoma. Physical examination reveals asymmetric atrophy of the right hemipelvis and proximal thigh muscles consistent with his prior poliomyelitis, and a large deep perianal mass.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the pelvis reveals a large (7.2 x 7.9 x 15.5 cm) multilocular, hypoattenuating retrorectal cystic lesion that displaces the rectum and rectosigmoid anteriorly without invading the prostate, seminal vesicles, or major adjacent pelvic vessels. CT additionally reveals a separate collection of smaller contiguous cysts in the left ischioanal fossa and left perineal subcutaneous fat, running parallel and adjacent to the left puborectalis muscle and breaching the left levator ani. No lesions are identified elsewhere in the abdominal cavity.

An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/CT (PET/CT) scan demonstrates no abnormal tracer uptake within either lesion, and no regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastases are present. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals the retrorectal mass to have intermediate signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences with multiple internal T1-hypointense and T2-hyperintense foci. The separate left ischioanal fossa collection demonstrates low T1 and high T2 signal intensity with multiple internal cysts and a T1/T2 hypointense rim, exhibiting thin peripheral enhancement without any enhancing mural solid component or osseous involvement.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Tailgut cyst correctly accounted for the benign multilocular retrorectal retro-cystic mass, but failed to explain the separate contiguous cluster of smaller cysts infiltrating the left ischioanal fossa and subcutaneous perineum.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The histopathologic examination of the resected retrorectal cyst revealed a benign tailgut cyst.

case_prompt:
A 34-year-old man with no previously diagnosed medical conditions presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of high fever, myalgias, nausea, and vomiting, accompanied by right upper quadrant abdominal pain. He denied cough, dyspnea, sore throat, or other respiratory symptoms. He reported no diarrhea, constipation, or urinary complaints. Three months prior to presentation, he had traveled to Pakistan.

On physical examination, the patient was febrile with a body temperature of 39.6 °C, heart rate of 148 beats per minute, blood pressure of 109/72 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 97% on ambient room air. He was visibly jaundiced. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right hypochondrium without guarding or rebound tenderness. Cardiovascular exam showed regular tachycardia without murmurs. Pulmonary examination was clear to auscultation.

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed leukopenia with a white blood cell count of 3,600/μL, absolute lymphopenia of 200/μL, hemoglobin of 14.5 g/dL, and marked thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 30,000/μL. Markers of hemolysis were prominent, including an elevated lactate dehydrogenase of 481 U/L and an undetectable haptoglobin (<10 mg/dL). Liver biochemistries showed direct hyperbilirubinemia with total bilirubin of 7.66 mg/dL and direct bilirubin of 4.27 mg/dL. Inflammatory and metabolic markers were profoundly elevated: C-reactive protein was 238 mg/L, procalcitonin was 61.30 ng/L, ferritin was 1,831.0 μg/L, D-dimer was 5.40 mg/L, and lactic acid was 2.4 mmol/L. An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia. A plain chest radiograph was unremarkable. Bedside abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic hepatic parenchyma with prominent periportal tracts and no evidence of cholelithiasis or biliary dilation.

On physical examination at triage, both patients appeared severely fatigued, febrile, and dehydrated. Examination was notable for diffuse myalgias, arthralgias, and abdominal discomfort without localized peritonitis. Neither patient had evidence of overt external mucosal hemorrhage or skin petechiae on initial physical evaluation.

A 46-year-old previously healthy adult presented for evaluation of progressive, inflammatory-type lumbar back pain persisting for the previous two months in the context of deterioration of general condition. The clinical interview revealed a potential close contact exposure to an individual with a chronic respiratory illness six months prior. The patient had no other past medical or surgical history.

On physical examination, the patient was conscious, alert, and in discomfort when mobilizing. Spinal examination demonstrated exquisite tenderness on palpation over the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine, accompanied by marked spinal stiffness and restricted range of motion. There were no motor, sensory, or reflex deficits in the lower extremities, and bowel and bladder function were preserved.

Initial laboratory workup demonstrated elevated systemic inflammatory markers: C-reactive protein was 58 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 60 mm in the first hour. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) screening serology was negative. A plain chest radiograph was normal without infiltrates or apical cavitary lesions. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated destructive multilevel spondylodiscitis involving the 10th, 11th, and 12th dorsal vertebrae and the 1st lumbar vertebra, associated with prominent bilateral abscess collections within both psoas muscles.

An 18-year-old previously healthy female presented with a 1-week history of right-sided painful neck swelling, fever, and odynophagia. She denied preceding pharyngitis, constitutional symptoms, night sweats, or known sick contacts. She reported no symptoms of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism, and had no history of neck trauma.

On physical examination, her blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg, pulse rate 89 beats/min, and temperature 37.0°C. She appeared clinically euthyroid without orbitopathy or stigmata of autoimmune thyroid disease. Examination of the neck revealed a right anterolateral mass measuring 4 x 5 cm that was mildly warm and tender to palpation, without fluctuance. There was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory evaluation revealed leukocytosis with a total white blood cell count of 17.6 x 10^9/L and neutrophil predominance. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 98 mm/hr and C-reactive protein was markedly elevated at 105.8 mg/L (reference <5.0). Screening for HIV was negative, and fasting blood glucose was 5.1 mmol/L. Baseline thyroid function tests showed a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level of 0.13 mIU/L (reference 0.56–4.90) and free thyroxine (FT4) of 21.1 pmol/L (reference 1.5–22.7).

Chest radiography demonstrated clear lung fields without infiltrates or adenopathy. Bedside neck ultrasound showed a heterogeneous appearance of both thyroid lobes, with a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass occupying the right lobe and extending toward the left isthmus-thyroid junction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a multiloculated hypodense rim-enhancing collection centered in the right thyroid lobe measuring 3.5 x 4.6 x 5.4 cm, with posterosuperior extracapsular extension into the prevertebral space measuring 5.5 cm craniocaudally from C2/3 to C6/7 and tracheal displacement to the left, accompanied by bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Fibreoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a patent airway without evidence of a pyriform sinus fistula.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Although subacute thyroiditis causes tender thyroid enlargement and transient thyrotoxicosis, it is a self-limiting nonsuppurative granulomatous inflammation and does not form large multiloculated necrotic abscesses or yield frank purulent aspirate.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: She underwent a bedside fine needle aspiration which aspirated 5 cc of frank pus and a repeat ultrasound guided aspiration which aspirated 25 cc of pus.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A rapidly expanding necrotic neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy raises concern for thyroid malignancy, but histopathological examination of the resected lobe showed xanthogranulomatous inflammation and microabscesses without malignant cellular atypia.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Tissue histopathological examination (HPE) demonstrated xanthogranulomatous inflammation with microabscess formation. No epithelioid histiocytes, granuloma formation nor Langhan's giant cells was seen.

case_prompt:
A 55-year-old male residing in Guangxi, China, presented with recurrent fever and exertional dyspnea of 2 weeks' duration. His medical history was significant for renal hypertension, uremia, and chronic hepatitis B virus infection. He had undergone allograft kidney transplantation 3.5 months earlier and was maintained on triple antirejection therapy with tacrolimus 3 mg every 12 hours, mycophenolate mofetil 0.5 g every 12 hours, and prednisone 30 mg daily.

On physical examination upon admission, his maximum temperature was 39.5°C. Chest auscultation revealed localized moist rales over the left lower lung. Dermatological examination revealed multifocal areas of skin breakdown and ulceration on the penis.

Laboratory investigations revealed severe pancytopenia: white blood cell count 1.25 x 10^9/L (93% neutrophils, 6% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 70 g/L, and platelet count 30.9 x 10^9/L. Serum albumin was 24.9 g/L, alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 31 U/L, and serum creatinine 76 µmol/L. Inflammatory markers demonstrated procalcitonin of 1.86 ng/mL and C-reactive protein >192 mg/L. Cellular immune profiling demonstrated profound T-cell depletion with CD3+ count of 61 cells/µL and CD4+ count of 35 cells/µL. Quantitative immunoglobulins and complements showed IgA 2.55 g/L, IgM 0.44 g/L, IgG 12.25 g/L, C3 0.626 g/L, and C4 0.183 g/L. Arterial blood gas analysis on mechanical ventilation (FiO2 56%) showed pH 7.42, PaO2 76 mmHg, PaCO2 23 mmHg, and base excess 8.0 mmol/L. Direct fluorescent fungal staining of sputum revealed fungal hyphae and spores. Chest CT demonstrated severe bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Profound CD4 depletion (<50 cells/µL) and severe acute respiratory distress syndrome raised high suspicion for PJP, prompting empirical trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, but direct fungal smear showing spores/hyphae, genital cutaneous lesions, and blood NGS identified disseminated Talaromyces marneffei.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Low-level CMV viremia (9.70 x 10^2 copies) was detected in this severely immunosuppressed host, but the presence of visible fungal structures on sputum fluorescent staining, cutaneous ulcerations, and high inflammatory markers indicated invasive fungal infection rather than isolated viral pneumonitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: On the patient's sputum smear, the fungal fluorescent staining was positive, and hyphae and spores could be seen.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: While Acinetobacter baumannii was subsequently cultured from sputum in the setting of elevated procalcitonin (1.86 ng/mL), antibacterial coverage failed to halt clinical deterioration as the primary systemic pathogen was disseminated dimorphic fungus.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Acinetobacter baumannii was cultured from the patient's sputum.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (NGS) of peripheral blood demonstrated sequence reads of Talaromyces marneffei (TM) in a severely immunosuppressed transplant recipient from endemic Guangxi presenting with fever, pancytopenia, cutaneous lesions, and severe ARDS.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: the NGS using the patient's peripheral blood revealed human polyomavirus Type 1 (BK polyomavirus) of 5098, sporozoan of 378, TM of 20, and human herpesvirus type 5 of 654.

editor_comments: Disseminated talaromycosis with severe ARDS, pancytopenia, and characteristic skin lesions in an early post-kidney transplant recipient from Guangxi. Admission breakpoint placed prior to blood metagenomic NGS and sputum bacterial culture.

A 25-year-old female presented with dull left mid-back pain of 3 months' duration. The pain was moderate in intensity and radiated anteriorly toward the left breast and precordium. Physical examination revealed focal tenderness over the inferior angle of the left scapula and 7th costovertebral junction, without overlying soft-tissue swelling or erythema. Neurological examination was normal.

Laboratory investigations demonstrated an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 40 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 6 mg/L. Serological testing for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody was negative.

Anteroposterior plain radiographs of the thoracic spine demonstrated left-sided scalloping of the T7 vertebral body, with cortical erosion of the left T7 pedicle and the adjacent rib head. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thoracic spine revealed a left-sided T7 enhancing periarticular erosive lesion, marked bone marrow edema in the posteromedial aspect of the left 7th rib, the left posterolateral T7 vertebral body, and the lateral left T7 pedicle. There was associated thickening and enhancement of the synovium of the left 7th costotransverse joint, with an enhancing soft-tissue mass elevating the overlying pleura and directly abutting the descending aorta.

A 36-year-old female presented with high fever of 15 days' duration, upper abdominal pain and limb muscle soreness for 7 days, and rapidly progressive shortness of breath for 4 days. Her peak temperature reached 41.0°C, accompanied by chills and sore throat. Prior outpatient treatment at another facility with oseltamivir and imipenem/cilastatin failed to halt progression of respiratory symptoms and worsening bilateral lung infiltrates. Her medical history was notable only for epilepsy controlled on lamotrigine and escitalopram. She had no preceding chronic cough or night sweats.

On arrival at the emergency department, she was in severe respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 36 breaths/min and oxygen saturation of 85% on a 10 L/min reservoir mask. Heart rate was 110 beats/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, and temperature 38.6°C. Physical examination revealed scleral icterus, moderate abdominal distension, and hepatomegaly. She was urgently intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation. Arterial blood gas analysis on 100% FiO2 revealed pH 7.376, PaO2 74.4 mmHg, PaCO2 59.4 mmHg, and an oxygenation index (PaO2/FiO2) of 74.4.

Laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count of 3.8 x 10^9/L (45.1% neutrophils, 50.7% lymphocytes), procalcitonin 0.25 ng/mL, and C-reactive protein 24.3 mg/L. Liver biochemistries demonstrated total bilirubin of 80.97 µmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 143 U/L, and aspartate aminotransferase 296 U/L. On physical examination, the infant is febrile, irritable, and icteric. The abdomen is distended, and hepatomegaly is present on palpation. No cutaneous eschar, rash, or petechiae are noted. Vital signs reveal an axillary temperature of 39.3 °C, a pulse rate of 176 beats per minute, and a respiratory rate of 46 breaths per minute.

Initial laboratory evaluation reveals a white blood cell count of 24.76 × 10^9/L (with 76.4% lymphocytes, 12.1% neutrophils, and 8.1% monocytes). Biochemical testing demonstrates marked transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia: total bilirubin 87.4 µmol/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 336.6 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 1317.1 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 1477.6 U/L.

Lumbar puncture reveals cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with a white blood cell count of 283 × 10^6/L (with 95.1% mononuclear cells and 4.9% polymorphonuclear neutrophils), a protein concentration of 3.084 g/L, and a glucose concentration of 1.18 mmol/L.

Computed tomography (CT) of the head shows patchy low-density areas in the bilateral frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes.

On the third day of admission, his seizures and jaundice had subsided, but the fever persisted, and the CSF still showed abnormalities.

A 32-year-old woman presents to the Ear, Nose and Throat clinic with a 2-week history of a tender lump on the right side of her upper neck. She had an initial mild fever, but reports no loss of appetite, weight loss, night sweats, cough, chest pain, nasal obstruction, or otologic symptoms. She has no known contact history with sick individuals. She previously received a course of amoxicillin for presumptive cervical lymphadenitis from a general practitioner, but the neck lump persisted.

On physical examination, a firm, mildly tender mass measuring 1.5 × 1 cm is palpable in the right upper neck. Nasal endoscopy reveals an irregular nasopharyngeal mass with overlying yellowish secretions, almost obliterating the fossa of Rosenmüller bilaterally. The remainder of the ear, nose, and throat examination is unremarkable.

Ultrasound of the neck demonstrates multiple enlarged hypoechoic cervical nodes bilaterally with distortion of the fatty hilum. Computed tomography (CT) of the nasopharynx and neck shows a heterogeneously enhancing soft tissue mass measuring 2.0 × 1.4 × 3.9 cm in the nasopharynx that obliterates the bilateral fossa of Rosenmüller and extends inferiorly to the upper oropharynx, accompanied by multiple homogeneously enhancing cervical nodes on both sides. Visualized lung apices show minimal consolidation and centrilobular nodules with a tree-in-bud appearance.

Baseline laboratory evaluation shows a white blood cell count of 6.99 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 70.4%, lymphocytes 19%), hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 60 mm/h. Anti-HIV and hepatitis B surface antigen tests are negative.

The liver and spleen are not palpable. There is 3+ bilateral peripheral pitting edema. Stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, palmar erythema, spider angiomatosis) are absent.

Initial laboratory evaluation reveals a microcytic, hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, hematocrit 30.8%) with anisopoikilocytosis. Platelet count is 305 × 10^3/µL and white blood cell count is 7.92 × 10^3/µL (80% neutrophils, 9.3% lymphocytes). Chest CT reveals extensive bilateral infiltrates with a tree-in-bud configuration. Abdominal/pelvic CT demonstrates marked ascites, colonic wall thickening, omental thickening, peritoneal thickening, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy, without hepatosplenomegaly or cirrhosis. Routine hematological and biochemical laboratory tests are completely unremarkable. Plain abdominal radiography is normal. Transabdominal ultrasound reveals a deformed gallbladder with localized thickening of its wall, without evidence of cholelithiasis or acoustic shadowing.

case_prompt:
A 42-year-old male farmer from the Eastern Province of Sri Lanka presents to a hospital on Day 4 of an acute febrile illness with high fever, severe frontal headache, rigors, and drenching cold sweats. His recent travel history is notable for return from West Africa three days prior to symptom onset, having resided for several weeks in Mali and Benin in rudimentary shelters with heavy mosquito exposure and inadequate netting, where multiple cohort members suffered acute febrile illnesses and one died of an unexplained fever. Routine screening performed at point of entry upon airport arrival was non-reactive.

On physical examination, he appears acutely toxic, febrile, and diaphoretic with chills. He has no cutaneous purpura or overt mucosal bleeding. Baseline laboratory evaluation demonstrates profound thrombocytopenia with low platelet counts on consecutive daily measurements, leading to inpatient admission under strict protocols for an acute viral vector-borne hemorrhagic syndrome.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as the leading presumptive diagnosis due to acute high fever, chills, rigors, severe headache, and marked thrombocytopenia in an area with high dengue endemicity. Excluded by negative dengue antibody testing and recovery of platelet counts alongside direct demonstration of blood parasites.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He was referred on day 4 to a Government Peripheral Hospital with suspicion for dengue fever. In view of clinical suspicion for rapid dengue progression, the attending doctor transferred the patient to Batticaloa Teaching Hospital in line with current policy of dengue management in Sri Lanka.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute Viral Hemorrhagic Fever of West African Origin
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because the patient lived in crude shelters in West Africa where several peers fell acutely ill and one cohort member died of an unidentified febrile illness. Excluded by absence of hemorrhagic manifestations and confirmation of protozoal parasitemia.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: During his time in Benin, the farmer recalled a heavy presence of mosquitoes and regular episodes of fever among the smuggled cohort. Smugglers had refused medical assistance in fear of alerting authorities. One death of a person due to "fever-like illness" was also reported although no medical details were available.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because P. vivax was historically the predominant species in Sri Lanka. Excluded when repeat RDT was positive for P. falciparum-specific HRP2 and blood smear showed characteristic high-density ring forms.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: For Plasmodium vivax infections, treatment consists of chloroquine for 3 days and primaquine for 14 days.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point occurred when repeat CareStart RDT and Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood smear microscopy demonstrated heavy infection with Plasmodium falciparum (0.7% parasitemia with 36,180 asexual parasites/µL, featuring double chromatin rings and applique trophozoite forms), resolving completely with artemether-lumefantrine and primaquine.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: By the end of day 7, venous blood was submitted to the hospital laboratory for RDT testing (CareStart) and microscopic examination. The slides were later sent to reference laboratory at AMC in Colombo for confirmation. Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films were examined for the detection of malarial parasites. The RDT was positive for P. falciparum and was confirmed by the microscopy (double chromatin ring stage and "applique" form of trophozoites), and the parasite density was calculated as 36,180 asexual parasites/microL, which equals 0.7% of red blood cell infected.

Approximately 1 month prior to presentation, he had been admitted to a local facility with high fever and rigors, where he received an empirical 3-day course of intravenous ceftriaxone and amikacin without any antiparasitic treatment. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain performed at the prior facility was unremarkable, and symptomatic therapies provided no relief.

On physical examination upon admission, he was afebrile, conscious, alert, and oriented to time, place, and person, though with a mildly reduced attention span. Vital signs revealed a pulse rate of 72 beats per minute, blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. Superficial reflexes were normal, and plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. Deep tendon reflexes were normal in the upper extremities but exaggerated in the lower extremities, with bilateral pendular knee jerks. Finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin, dysdiadochokinesia, and tandem gait testing were all markedly impaired bilaterally. Nystagmus and signs of meningeal irritation were absent.

Core Clinical Tension: A 20-year-old female agricultural worker in rural southern Laos presents with a 2-week history of severe headache and high fever with myalgia and vomiting that failed oral cephalosporin therapy. The physical examination is completely normal without a characteristic eschar or petechial exanthem. This presentation embodies the classic diagnostic dilemma of undifferentiated acute tropical febrile illness, where scrub typhus and murine typhus share identical clinical features and frequently occur as unrecognized coinfections.

Admission Breakpoint: Admission triage encompasses exposure history (rural rice farming, vegetable gardens in Laos), 14 days of headache, 3 days of fever, vomiting, failed oral cephalexin therapy, admission vital signs (temperature 38.5 C), physical exam documenting absence of rash or eschar, and initial negative malaria screening. Murine typhus is considered as an endemic cause of flea-borne tropical fever, but molecular diagnostics revealed concurrent Orientia tsutsugamushi infection.

Her residence was bordered by agricultural vegetable gardens. Prior to presentation, she had completed a 5-day course of oral cephalexin without clinical improvement.

On physical examination upon admission, her body temperature was 38.5 C. Blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate were stable. Detailed dermatological and systemic examination was entirely unremarkable; specifically, there was no cutaneous rash, and thorough inspection of the skin revealed no inoculation eschar. Rapid and microscopic screening tests for hemoparasites were negative.

A 24-year-old previously healthy man, who had immigrated from Ethiopia six years prior, presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of intermittent, involuntary shaking of his left leg. He had received an undocumented 2-month course of medications from a primary care provider with partial relief, but had subsequently discontinued therapy. Over the preceding 6 months, he developed progressive gait unsteadiness and intentional tremors of the right upper limb. During the month prior to presentation, he experienced a severe resurgence of holocranial headache, projectile vomiting, and fever. There was no history of seizures, altered sensorium, visual changes, or cranial nerve weakness. Past medical history was unremarkable, with no high-risk sexual behavior; his mother had received a 9-month course of antimicrobial therapy for a chronic pulmonary infection 15 years earlier.

Deep tendon reflexes were symmetric, with an exaggerated pendular knee jerk in the right leg. Sensory examination was normal. Right cerebellar testing revealed marked intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, past-pointing, and dysmetria. His gait was wide-based and ataxic, with a pronounced tendency to lurch toward the right.

A purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test revealed an induration of 16 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed an intra-axial, well-defined parenchymal lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated marked peripheral ring enhancement with central diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated elevated lipid and lactate peaks.

He reported no chest pain, palpitations, hemoptysis, rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or altered mental status. He noted a history of a treated tropical febrile infection while living in India one year earlier, managed with antimicrobial and anti-relapse therapy. He reported no recent international travel, no recent insect or animal bites, and no history of blood transfusions.

On physical examination, he was febrile with a body temperature of 39.9°C and tachycardic with a heart rate of 136 beats/min. His blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% while breathing ambient air. Oropharyngeal examination revealed tonsillar and posterior pharyngeal erythema without exudates. There was no cervical or peripheral lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurological examinations were otherwise normal, with no hepatosplenomegaly or meningeal signs.

Initial triage laboratory investigations revealed a prominent neutrophilic leukocytosis. A portable plain chest radiograph showed clear lung fields without consolidation, pleural effusion, or pulmonary vascular congestion.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute viral respiratory tract infection (COVID-19) alone
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because the patient presented during an endemic wave with cough, pharyngeal erythema, and confirmed positive nasopharyngeal RT-PCR. However, despite resolution of pharyngitis and cough after three days of supportive care, the patient experienced abrupt recrudescent fever spikes (39.1°C) with classic shaking rigors and diaphoresis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A working diagnosis of mild COVID-19 upper respiratory tract infection was made. The patient was started on treatment based on the local COVID-19 management protocol at the time. After treatment for 3 days, there was resolution of cough and pharyngeal erythema, however, on the 4th day patient started to spike high-grade fever of 39.1 degree Celsius.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because an acute high-grade fever spike to 39.1°C with neutrophilic leukocytosis and rigors in a diabetic patient raised immediate concern for hospital-acquired or secondary pyogenic bacteremia. However, comprehensive blood cultures remained completely sterile.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Sepsis screen was ordered. The blood cultures were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Persistent paroxysmal rigors and sweats prompted microscopic evaluation of thick and thin peripheral blood films, which revealed ring forms and developing trophozoites of Plasmodium vivax at 0.1% parasitemia, establishing a hypnozoite reactivation relapse triggered by intercurrent viral infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A blood smear was done to rule out malaria. Blood smears showed ring and trophozoites of P. vivax at 0.1% (Figure 1).

editor_comments: Plasmodium vivax malaria relapse with hypnozoite reactivation triggered by intercurrent mild COVID-19 infection. All pathogen names, send-out PCR panels, blood culture results, and peripheral smears excluded from case_prompt.

case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman presented to the gastroenterology service with a two-month history of progressive odynophagia and high dysphagia, accompanied by a 5-kg weight loss. Her symptoms had advanced from difficulty swallowing solids to total dysphagia for both solid and liquid foods, complicated by sialorrhea, marked physical asthenia, and night sweats. Her medical history was notable for ileocolonic inflammatory bowel disease diagnosed 13 years earlier, currently in clinical remission, with associated spondylitis and sacroiliitis. She had previously received biological therapy with a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor combined with azathioprine, which was discontinued five years prior; she was then maintained on mesalazine (3 g/day) and azathioprine (100 mg/day). Eleven months before presentation, treatment with a second tumor necrosis factor inhibitor was initiated, but this was discontinued one month prior to admission because of recurrent sore throat. Two months before presentation, she was treated for acute erythematous angina with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid without improvement, and subsequent outpatient antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone similarly failed to relieve her symptoms.

On physical examination, she appeared underweight with impaired general condition. Her temperature was 36.9°C, blood pressure was normal, weight was 48 kg, height was 164 cm, and body mass index was 17.85 kg/m². Her skin and oral mucous membranes were pale and dehydrated. Examination of the musculoskeletal system revealed pain on mobilization of the pelvis and lumbar spine, with positive Eriksen and Volkman signs. Palpation of the superficial lymph node basins revealed two firm, immobile, non-tender oval structures, each measuring approximately 1 cm in greatest diameter, in the right laterocervical region. Chest auscultation was clear without added sounds. Otorhinolaryngological examination revealed bilaterally congested and hypertrophic palatine tonsils with multiple small, gray-whitish granules diffusely disseminated across the pharynx and larynx.

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed moderate microcytic hypochromic anemia, lymphopenia, and mild hypoalbuminemia. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was markedly elevated at 120 mm/h (reference: 2–12), C-reactive protein was 88.24 mg/L (reference: 0–5), prothrombin index was 61% (reference: 79–146%), and the international normalized ratio was 1.38 (reference: 0.8–1.16). Routine serum biochemistries, renal function, and liver profiles were within normal limits.

case_prompt:
A 49-year-old man from Guangxi, China, presented to the hospital with a seven-month history of cough, fever, and progressive emaciation, and a one-month history of an enlarging mass on the left side of his neck. He had received intravenous ceftazidime at an outside hospital, which temporarily resolved his fever, but the cervical mass continued to expand. He had no history of previous medical illness and took no regular medications.

On physical examination at admission, his body temperature was 38.0°C. Examination of the head and neck revealed two palpable masses: one located on the left lateral neck and the other in the right submental area. The left cervical mass measured 8 cm in diameter; both masses were erythematous, inflamed, and tender to palpation. Auscultation of the chest revealed moist rales localized to the upper lobe of the left lung. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 14,200/µL with 12,200 neutrophils/µL and 1,390 lymphocytes/µL, a hemoglobin level of 124 g/L, and a platelet count of 167,000/µL. Inflammatory markers were elevated, with a C-reactive protein level of 167.04 mg/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 70 mm/h, and a procalcitonin level of 0.61 ng/mL. Flow cytometric analysis of lymphocyte subsets demonstrated total CD3+, CD4+, and CD8+ T-lymphocyte counts of 1,137 cells/µL, 470 cells/µL, and 620 cells/µL, respectively. Serum liver enzymes, renal function parameters, and total serum immunoglobulins were within normal limits. The serum galactomannan index was 0.35, and an immunoassay for human immunodeficiency virus was negative. Computed tomography of the neck showed mixed-density lesions on the left side of the neck and in the right submental region.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Rapid enlargement of tender, fluctuant cervical masses with neutrophilic leukocytosis suggested bacterial lymphadenitis, and initial pus cultures did recover Burkholderia cepacia; however, despite susceptibility-guided antibacterial therapy, the patient developed worsening pulmonary consolidations and endobronchial lesions driven by an underlying dimorphic fungus.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: B. cepacia was cultured from the mass on the neck and submental pus after 1 week.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Subacute febrile pulmonary consolidation and pulmonary nodules in a debilitated patient raised concern for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, but the serum galactomannan index was normal.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The galactomannan index was 0.35, and the patient was HIV negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A solitary 8-cm cervical mass associated with profound weight loss and submental lesions in an adult male suggested lymphoma or metastatic carcinoma, but bronchofibroscopic biopsy revealed inflammatory endobronchial nodules without malignant cytopathology.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Bronchofibroscopy revealed bronchial nodules in the left upper and lower lobes, obstructing the lumen, and mucosal hyperplasia and hypertrophy

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The definitive diagnosis was reached when bronchofibroscopy identified obstructive bronchial nodules and hilar lymphadenopathy, and fungal cultures along with next-generation sequencing confirmed Talaromyces marneffei from bronchial tissue, hilar lymph nodes, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid in a patient subsequently found to harbor neutralizing anti-interferon-gamma autoantibodies.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: TM (Figure 2) was cultured from a bronchial nodule, left hilar lymph node, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.

editor_comments: Complies fully with admission breakpoint principles. Triage presentation captures the full clinical history, exam, labs, and baseline neck CT while strictly omitting pus microbiology, bronchoscopic biopsy, fungal isolation, and autoantibody testing.

case_prompt:
A 44-year-old otherwise healthy Sri Lankan male presented to an outpatient clinic with a six-month history of swelling in his left ankle joint. He noted progressive swelling associated with stiffness, restricted range of movement, and discomfort during weight-bearing. He denied cough, dyspnea, fever, night sweats, or constitutional weight loss. There was no history of previous joint trauma, accidental injury, or surgical intervention.

On physical examination, the left ankle joint was visibly swollen, but there was no overlying warmth, erythema, or localized tenderness. There was global restriction of active and passive movements at the ankle joint. The systemic physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Basic hematological indices, including complete blood count, were normal, though the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly elevated at 35 mm in the first hour. Fasting blood glucose was within normal limits, and a screening test for human immunodeficiency virus was negative. A plain chest radiograph showed clear lung fields without infiltrates, consolidation, or cavitary lesions.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Chronic insidious joint swelling with restricted mobility and elevated inflammatory markers suggested an inflammatory arthropathy, but comprehensive serological testing including rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody was entirely negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Arthritis workup with rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody (anti-CCP), and antinuclear antibody (ANA) was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Progressive joint destruction and disability could suggest a indolent pyogenic joint infection, but the classical signs of bacterial sepsis—including local erythema, warmth, severe joint tenderness, systemic pyrexia, and peripheral leukocytosis—were distinctly absent.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: On examination, his left ankle joint was swollen without tenderness or warmth

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Chronic weight-bearing pain and limited range of motion in an ankle joint could represent post-traumatic or degenerative osteoarthrosis, but there was no preceding history of mechanical injury or surgery, and advanced imaging demonstrated subarticular osteitis and inflammatory marrow edema.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Patient did not have a history of previous trauma or surgery.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic breakthrough was achieved when an open synovial biopsy revealed granulomatous inflammation, and definitive automated culture of the synovial tissue grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis, confirming primary tuberculous arthritis of the ankle.

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 35-year-old female bank employee presented to the emergency department complaining of a five-day history of high-grade fever of a waxing-and-waning nature, associated with vomiting, generalized body aches, and progressive somnolence. The fever had begun during her mandatory hotel quarantine seven days after returning from a vacation in Sudan, during which she did not take any chemoprophylactic medication. She had not improved despite symptomatic treatment with antipyretics and antiemetics during quarantine. She reported a remote febrile illness ten years earlier while residing in an endemic region, but had no recent sick contacts among family or acquaintances.

On physical examination in the emergency department, she appeared lethargic, ill, and somnolent, with an oral temperature fluctuating up to 40.0°C. Respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation were monitored. A nasopharyngeal swab reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction test for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 was negative.

Initial laboratory investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 12.1 g/dL, a normal white blood cell count, and a platelet count of 150,000/µL. Serum liver biochemistries demonstrated hepatocellular injury with an aspartate aminotransferase of 58 U/L and an alanine aminotransferase of 57 U/L. The total serum bilirubin was elevated at 26 µmol/L. Serum creatinine and basic electrolytes were within acceptable limits.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: High-grade fever, somnolence, and systemic myalgias arising in mandatory travel quarantine strongly warranted exclusion of acute pandemic viral infection, but nasopharyngeal swab PCR was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Severe undulating fevers, lethargy, gastrointestinal upset, and transaminitis following international travel suggested acute bacterial septicemia or enteric fever, but serial blood cultures and urine cultures remained negative throughout hospitalization.

case_prompt:
A 45-year-old male immigrant from Mexico presented to the emergency department complaining of progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness of one month's duration, resulting in worsening difficulty ambulating. Over the preceding two weeks, he noted a loss of sensation below the nipple level, and during the past week, he developed urinary and stool retention. He denied cough, shortness of breath, chills, or documented fevers, but endorsed drenching night sweats over the past month.

Sensation to light touch and pinprick was markedly diminished below the T4–T5 dermatomal level. No peripheral lymphadenopathy was appreciated on general examination.

Initial emergency laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count of 12,600/µL, a platelet count of 494,000/µL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 2.6 mg/dL. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine demonstrated findings of osteomyelitis involving the T3, T4, and T5 vertebral levels with an associated epidural mass/abscess and extensive bony destruction of the T4 and T5 vertebral bodies, resulting in severe spinal canal stenosis and thoracic spinal cord compression.

case_prompt:
A 53-year-old male from Kerala, South India, presented to a tertiary hospital with a three-week history of watery, non-bloody loose stools occurring three to four times per day. He reported intermittent vague abdominal pain, decreased appetite, and a 3- to 4-kg weight loss over the preceding month. He denied fever, vomiting, respiratory symptoms, or acute urticaria. His past medical history was significant for alcohol use disorder, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia on regular medications for two years, as well as an ischemic stroke resulting in residual left hemiparesis two years prior. He also had a history of chronic cavitary pulmonary infection treated with multi-drug antimycobacterial therapy for the previous six months. He had no history of intravenous drug use, high-risk sexual behavior, or recent travel outside the state, and consumed only cooked food. He worked barefoot as a cattle farmer on his farm, which featured a shallow freshwater pond used for fish aquaculture; there was no known open-field defecation in the work area.

On physical examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. He had bilateral pitting pedal edema and a non-migratory macular erythematous rash over the anterior aspect of both lower legs of two weeks' duration. Abdominal and systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Routine laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 9.6 g/dL, an elevated total white blood cell count of 13,600/µL with 90% polymorphonuclear cells, 6% lymphocytes, 2% eosinophils, and 2% monocytes, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 78 mm/h. Serum electrolytes demonstrated marked hypokalemia with a potassium level of 2.6 mEq/L. Random blood glucose at admission was markedly elevated at 274 mg/dL. Screening for human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibodies was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated fatty hepatomegaly with focal hepatic lesions. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed several hypodense lesions in segment 5 of the liver with mild hepatomegaly. Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated bilateral upper lobe cavitary lesions. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed and revealed normal mucosal findings.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and leukocytosis led to the isolation of Aeromonas sobria on stool bacteriological culture; however, antibacterial therapy failed to arrest the underlying illness because the bacteria were opportunistic secondary invaders crossing an intestinal mucosa disrupted by nematode hyperinfection.

diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Stool occult blood (Hemospot kit, standard guaiac method, Tulip Diagnostics, Goa, India) and Clostridium difficile toxin (VIDAS difficile toxin A and B, bioMerieux SA) were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Weight loss, anorexia, chronic diarrhea, and hypodense hepatic lesions on abdominal CT raised high concern for occult gastrointestinal malignancy with metastatic dissemination, but upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal, and the liver lesions reflected fatty/inflammatory changes in the setting of chronic alcohol use and systemic illness.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed, which was normal.

He is normotensive, a non-smoker, and non-diabetic, with no history of previous intravascular catheterization or surgical procedures.

On physical examination, his body temperature is 38.0°C and he has a distinct, tender pulsatile mass in the periumbilical abdominal region.

Baseline laboratory evaluation reveals a significant leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 20,000/mm3 (reference range 3,000–11,000) and an elevated C-reactive protein.

Abdominal ultrasonography reveals mild hepatosplenomegaly and multiple significantly enlarged, heterogeneous, necrotic, conglomerate retroperitoneal lymph nodes involving the periportal and peripancreatic regions. Color Doppler interrogation demonstrates multiple variable-sized aneurysms of the abdominal aorta with central pulsatile turbulent flow and peripheral laminated thrombus. Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic angiography of the abdomen reveals two distinct saccular aneurysms with thin, irregular walls arising from the abdominal aorta: a suprarenal aneurysm measuring 5.2 × 2.5 cm and an infrarenal aneurysm measuring 4.5 × 4.0 cm, with near-total compression of the right renal artery producing chronic ischemic renal parenchymal changes. Multiple enlarged necrotic para-aortic lymph nodes (up to 2.8 cm in short axis) are identified immediately adjacent to the aneurysmal walls. Computed tomographic screening of the thorax is unremarkable, and no abnormal bowel wall thickening or discrete gastrointestinal masses are observed.

Four months prior to this presentation, he had been evaluated for similar but more severe symptoms of hemoptysis, dyspnea, night sweats, and fatigue, and was started on a multi-drug antimycobacterial regimen consisting of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. His occupational history was notable for working for seven years in a local gemstone mine, where occupational exposure to silica dust was prevalent during gem mining.

On presentation, the patient was ill-appearing and in respiratory distress. Initial vital signs demonstrated an oxygen saturation of 75% on ambient air, a body temperature of 38.9 C, and a blood pressure of 136/68 mmHg. Physical examination of the respiratory system revealed labored breathing, poor air movement, and coarse crackles with expiratory wheezing throughout bilateral lung fields. The patient was euvolemic. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable, with normal heart sounds and no jugular venous distension. Abdominal and dermatologic examinations were normal. A chest radiograph could not be obtained due to resource scarcity.

A 60-year-old woman presented to the outpatient surgical clinic complaining of a painless mass in her right calf that had been present for two years. The mass was discovered incidentally two years earlier and had been diagnosed clinically at that time as a lipoma, for which no treatment was initiated. Over the preceding few months, the mass had gradually increased in size. Her medical history was notable for essential hypertension of ten years' duration managed with antihypertensive pharmacotherapy. Her past surgical history included a laparoscopic cholecystectomy ten years prior and an abdominal hysterectomy for uterine leiomyomas five years prior.

On physical examination, vital signs were normal. Examination of the right lower extremity revealed a 10 x 7 cm mass in the posterior compartment of the calf. The mass was soft, non-tender, fluctuant, and mobile from side to side without overlying warmth, erythema, or skin tethering.

Bedside and preoperative evaluation included a plain chest radiograph, which excluded pulmonary nodules or consolidations, and an abdominal ultrasound, which confirmed normal hepatic and visceral architecture without cysts or lesions. Soft tissue ultrasound of the right calf mass demonstrated a well-circumscribed cystic lesion containing multiple internal small cysts.

A 32-year-old male presented to the outpatient medical center complaining of an extensive, painless erythematous plaque involving his anterior neck and chest region that had been present for 9 years and had ulcerated 2 years prior to presentation. The lesions had initially appeared 9 years ago as small, asymptomatic papules and nodules on his neck for which he did not seek treatment. Over time, the lesions expanded into confluent plaques and nodules across the neck and chest and developed ulcerations with discharging tracts. He had previously been diagnosed with a cutaneous bacterial infection and completed empirical courses of systemic oral antibiotics and topical iodine without improvement. Over the preceding year, the patient experienced an unintentional 15-kg weight loss; however, he denied fevers, chills, productive cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, or arthralgias. Past medical history was notable for a treated chronic pulmonary infection 12 years prior, for which he had completed a 6-month multidrug antimicrobial regimen.

Physical examination revealed a 3 cm × 5 cm erythematous plaque with ulceration and friable granulation tissue on the chest wall. Surrounding the plaque were multiple 1 cm × 2 cm erythematous nodules and plaques draining via visible sinus tracts over the neck and chest. Palpation of the peripheral lymph node basins demonstrated multiple enlarged, mobile bilateral cervical and axillary lymph nodes measuring approximately 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm. The remainder of the systemic examination was normal.

Baseline laboratory investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 85 g/L (reference 130–175 g/L) indicating moderate normocytic anemia. Inflammatory markers were markedly elevated, with a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of 63.7 mg/L (reference < 5 mg/L) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 120 mm/h (reference < 15 mm/h). Serum biochemistry revealed an albumin of 30.6 g/L and an elevated globulin of 43.5 g/L. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA) and serum tumor markers were within normal reference ranges.

Superficial lymph node ultrasonography identified multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral neck and axillary regions with features of partial liquefactive abscess formation. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated moderate splenomegaly. Chest computed tomography (CT) demonstrated bilateral fibrous pulmonary foci and minor inflammatory changes in the lower lobe of the left lung, along with multiple mildly enlarged bilateral axillary lymph nodes.

He initially received oral corticosteroid therapy at an outside hospital, which produced no clinical improvement.

The patient reports no fever, chills, night sweats, cough, hemoptysis, fatigue, or unintended weight loss. He reports no dysuria, hematuria, or altered urinary stream. Medical history is negative for diabetes mellitus, malignancies, chronic renal failure, or known immunosuppression. He has no past history of mycobacterial infections or known exposure to infected individuals. He denies prior penile trauma, urological interventions, or high-risk sexual behavior.

On physical examination, the patient is afebrile and systemically well. Examination of the external genitalia reveals multiple well-defined, non-indurated, tender, punched-out ulcers measuring 0.5 to 1.0 cm in diameter with ragged, regular borders located along the coronal groove of the penis. The ulcer bases are covered with yellowish purulent discharge. No palpable superficial inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy is present. Other mucocutaneous surfaces and general physical examination findings are completely normal.

Initial diagnostic evaluation reveals normal urine microscopy. Bedside ultrasound of the genitourinary system and regional superficial lymph node basins demonstrates normal anatomy without lymphadenopathy or pelvic collections.

Six days prior to transfer, she developed acute-onset high fever peaking at 39.6°C, accompanied by chills, shivering, cough, sputum production, fatigue, and dyspnea. She also noted an extensive rash involving her face, chest, and groin. At an outside hospital, initial chest computed tomography, urinary ultrasound, and brain magnetic resonance imaging showed no acute abnormalities. Treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone, clindamycin, and methylprednisolone resulted in resolution of her respiratory symptoms, but high spiking fevers persisted unabated.

Her past medical history was notable for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic mild anemia; her daughter had a history of thalassemia.

On physical examination upon admission, the patient was febrile and appeared moderately ill. A maculopapular rash was visible over the face, anterior chest, and inguinal regions. Abdominal examination revealed non-tender hepatosplenomegaly, which was confirmed on abdominal color Doppler ultrasound and repeat chest/abdominal CT.

Laboratory studies demonstrated marked pancytopenia with decreased white blood cells, red blood cells, hemoglobin, and platelets. Serum ferritin was markedly elevated, while concentrations of serum folic acid and vitamin B12 were within normal parameters. An initial bone marrow aspiration revealed a low proliferation rate of nucleated cells, a decreased myeloid-to-erythroid ratio, abnormal erythroblast morphology, decreased marrow iron stores, and impaired megakaryocyte platelet production.

case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of intermittent fevers, progressive abdominal distension, and drenching night sweats. She underwent renal transplantation 8 years prior and has been maintained on triple immunosuppressive therapy consisting of tacrolimus (2 mg morning, 1.5 mg evening), mycophenolate mofetil (360 mg morning, 180 mg evening), and methylprednisolone (8 mg daily). She denies acute gastrointestinal bleeding or altered bowel habits.

On physical examination, the patient appears chronically ill and cachectic, with a height of 155 cm and weight of 40 kg. Vital signs demonstrate low-grade pyrexia. Cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations are within normal limits. Abdominal examination reveals visible abdominal distension with positive shifting dullness, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and involuntary rebound tenderness throughout all quadrants.

Initial laboratory evaluation demonstrates a white blood cell count of 4.23 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin of 76 g/L, and platelet count of 161 × 10⁹/L. Serum biochemistry shows albumin of 25 g/L, serum creatinine of 167 µmol/L, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 25.34 mL/min/1.75 m². Abdominal ultrasonography confirms moderate-to-large free ascites. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest reveals scattered patchy infiltrates throughout both lung fields and a left-sided pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracentesis yields clear-to-turbid fluid with a total leukocyte count of 0.677 × 10⁹/L (61% monocytes, 39% polymorphonuclear cells), total protein of 24 g/L, glucose of 6.45 mmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase of 155 U/L, and an adenosine deaminase (ADA) level of 7.6 U/L.

case_prompt:
A 9-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of persistent pain and progressive swelling over the medial aspect of his left foot of unclear etiology. The pain had progressively worsened to the point where he was unable to bear weight on the affected limb. His parents reported no history of fever, chills, anorexia, weight loss, or other systemic constitutional symptoms.

On physical examination, the child was afebrile and systemically well. Examination of the left foot revealed mild localized swelling and tenderness over the medial midfoot, centered at the talonavicular articulation. The range of motion of the left foot and ankle was painfully restricted, with significant discomfort elicited upon passive inversion and eversion. There were no overlying skin sinus tracts or erythema.

Initial hematological investigations were within normal limits except for a mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 30 mm/hr and a positive C-reactive protein (CRP) of 10 mg/L. Plain anteroposterior and oblique radiographs of the left foot demonstrated diffuse regional osteopenia, marginal erosions along the articular surfaces of the talus and navicular bones, narrowing of the talonavicular joint space, and prominent soft-tissue swelling medial to the talonavicular joint.

On histopathological examination, epitheloid granulomas with caseating necrosis were seen which was suggestive of tuberculosis (figure 2).
